stem: What is the gold standard diagnostic study for identifying malrotation in an infant with bilious vomiting?

options.text: Contrast upper gastrointestinal study to identify the duodenojejunal (DJ) junction
Ultrasound to measure the pyloric muscle thickness
Suction biopsy to assess for ganglion cells
Abdominal CT scan to assess bowel position

explanation: Contrast upper gastrointestinal study is the gold standard because it shows the position of the duodenojejunal junction and can confirm malrotation.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because a plain abdominal X-ray may show obstruction but cannot reliably confirm malrotation or the position of the DJ junction.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because contrast imaging of the upper gastrointestinal tract is used to identify the position of the DJ junction, which is the key diagnostic feature in malrotation.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because ultrasound measuring pyloric muscle thickness is used for pyloric stenosis, not for diagnosing malrotation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because suction biopsy is used to diagnose Hirschsprung disease by assessing ganglion cells, not malrotation.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because CT is not the standard first-line study for diagnosing malrotation in an infant with bilious vomiting.

source.hint: This study involves using a special dye to visualize the anatomy of the upper GI tract.
